name: evalens
description: See what a line of Python produced, painted beside the code — on demand, never as you type. No print(), no debugger, no notebook.

commands.title: Evalens: Toggle Follow in Values Panel

evalens.pythonPath.markdownDescription: Interpreter used to run the evaluation kernel. Empty means try the interpreter the Python extension has selected, then `python3`, then `python`, and use the first that runs and reports Python 3.9 or later. A path set here is never quietly replaced: if it does not work, Evalens says so instead of falling back.

evalens.progressDelay.markdownDescription: Milliseconds an evaluation must still be running before Evalens shows a cancellable progress notification. Almost every evaluation finishes in a few milliseconds, and a notification on each one would be intolerable — so the notification only appears once an evaluation has already failed to finish, which is the moment the extension otherwise looks like it ignored the keypress. Raising it buys a quieter window at the cost of a longer silence before anything confirms the keypress was heard, and before there is a Cancel button to press. `0` shows it immediately.

evalens.advanceSkipsComments.markdownDescription: Whether **Evalens: Evaluate and Advance** steps over comment lines on its way to the next statement. Leaving this on costs you the comment: in a file written to be read, the paragraph above a statement is the explanation, and the cursor goes past it without stopping. Turning it off buys that pause back at one extra keypress per comment block — and that press evaluates nothing, because a comment is not a statement. Blank lines and the body of a multi-line statement are always stepped over; only comments are a matter of taste.

evalens.printedLabel.markdownDescription: What the annotation calls the output a statement printed. The default word keeps the `label: value` grammar the rest of the annotation uses and says in plain English what the code did — `<stdout>` is jargon a first-year student has not met. Set `»` for a terse marker instead; it is the one that exists in every font VS Code falls back to on macOS, where `▸` and `▶` do not and render at a width that misaligns the lines the marker is there to clarify. `stderr` keeps its own name whatever this says.

enumDescriptions: Announce every result from Evaluate at Cursor and Evaluate and Advance.
Never announce; **Evalens: Announce Result at Cursor** still works when you ask for it.
evalens.announceResults.markdownDescription:
Whether an inline result is also announced, for a screen reader. An inline result is painted with a decoration, and the VS Code API gives a decoration no accessibility label of any kind — so without this, pressing the evaluate key produces silence that is indistinguishable from a dead keybinding. Announcing puts the same answer in a notification, which VS Code does read out, and keeps the last one in the status bar with an accessibility label on it. **The annotation is unchanged either way**; this adds a channel rather than moving the answer off the line.

`auto` follows `editor.accessibilitySupport`, announcing when it is set to `on`. VS Code exposes no way for an extension to ask whether a screen reader is attached, and its own auto-detection leaves that setting reading `auto` whether it found one or not — so if your screen reader works without setting it, choose `always` here.

A file load never announces whatever this says: two hundred annotations from one keypress would be worse than announcing nothing.

evalens.resultColumn.markdownDescription: Column to line inline results up on. `0` (the default) puts each result just after the code that produced it, following Rider, so nothing is pushed further right than it has to be. A fixed column makes a file of plain assignments read as two tidy columns, at the cost of a wide empty gap after every short line — and it stops helping as soon as a line carries more than one value. A line already past the column keeps its usual gap rather than being dragged out further.

evalens.loopValues.markdownDescription: Report every value a `for` loop's target held, rather than only the last one. On, a loop reads `p: 1, 2, 3, 4`; off, it reads `p: 4` like any other statement. The sequence is most of the reason to evaluate a loop at all, and it is also the longest thing Evalens ever paints on one line — turn it off if the loops in your files are long enough that the summary is noise. Off also stops the loop being rewritten to record itself, so it costs nothing to run.

evalens.loopIterations.markdownDescription: How many of a loop's iterations are listed before the rest are elided as `… (+9,994 more) …`. The final value is always shown whatever this says, because for a loop stopped by `break` it is the answer you were looking for. More iterations show the shape of a run more clearly, at the cost of an annotation that pushes the code off the right of the window, and of one more `repr()` kept per loop. Ignored while **Loop Values** is off.

evalens.readNames.markdownDescription: Report what the names on a line held, not only what the line produced. `print('y:', y)` produced `None`, and `y` is what the line was about — this is what puts `y: [1, 2, 3]` beside it. Turning it off leaves a bare result-only annotation, at the cost of having nothing to say on every line that is not a binding, which in a real file is most of them. Reading a name cannot run your code: it is a namespace lookup and nothing else.

evalens.readNamesPerLine.markdownDescription: How many of a line's names are annotated. More names per line, at the cost of a longer annotation on busy lines: a line mentioning eight variables reports eight values and the code disappears underneath them. Names are taken in the order the line reads them, so the ones dropped are the ones furthest right. Ignored while **Read Names** is off.

evalens.resetOnLoad.markdownDescription: Whether **Evalens: Evaluate File** clears the namespace before it runs the whole file, rather than running on top of whatever an earlier load left there. On (the default), a binding deleted from the file and reloaded is actually gone, and a second file cannot quietly read back a name an earlier one defined — the notebook trap this project exists to argue against. Off buys back the setup cost of a slow import block or a large cache built at the top of the file, at the price of the namespace remembering more than the file on screen defines; turn it off only for that specific workflow, and see **Evalens: Evaluate File** paint a status-bar note when it does. **Evaluate at Cursor** and **Evaluate and Advance** never reset, and a run over a selection never resets regardless of this setting — only a whole-file run does. **Evalens: Run File as Script** always resets, whatever this says, because it exists to answer whether the file matches `python3 file.py`, a question a carried-over namespace would make unanswerable.

evalens.valuesPanel.follow.markdownDescription: Whether the values panel scrolls the row that just changed into view, every time an evaluation lands. On (the default), the newest value is always what you see, which is the point of a panel that would otherwise keep showing whatever was on screen while new rows land out of sight below the fold. Off keeps your scroll position exactly where you left it — useful for reading back through a file's history without the view jumping away from it underneath you. **Evalens: Toggle Follow in Values Panel** flips this from the command palette or from the `$(unlock)` / `$(lock)` button in the values panel's own title bar, so you never have to leave the panel to turn it off mid-session.

evalens.valuesPanel.outputLines.markdownDescription: How many lines of a printed stream or a long value the values panel shows before folding the rest behind `Show all`, the way a notebook folds a long cell output — a nested loop printing ten thousand lines used to turn one row into a ten-thousand-line wall the panel could not scroll past. Fewer lines fold sooner, keeping the panel readable whatever a statement printed. More lines show a longer stretch of a run before you have to click through, at the cost of a taller row and a heavier rebuild, since the panel repaints every row in full on every evaluation. `Show all` — or a click on the block's own label — still shows everything, inside its own scrolling area, and `Open in editor` opens the untouched text as a plain document beside the panel. There is no setting to turn folding off entirely: an unfolded ten-thousand-line row is the defect this setting exists to prevent.

evalens.valuesPanel.followCursor.markdownDescription: Reveal corresponding values and source while navigating either pane, keeping keyboard focus where you are working. On (the default), learners can follow code and its captured results together. Off lets you browse independently; clicking a row or pressing Enter/Space still reveals its source. The Values panel checkbox changes this setting. Following newly evaluated results is controlled separately by `evalens.valuesPanel.follow`.

colors.description: Colour of an inline evaluation result.

Colour of a label an inline result introduces a value with: `x:`, the `=>` separator, the `…+N more` footnote and the reduced-context caveat. Deliberately dimmer than the value it introduces — contrast against the editor background is 3.97:1 dark, 3.55:1 light, 10.85:1 high contrast, 6.64:1 high contrast light, against the value's 7.15 / 5.03 / 13.03 / 8.04.

Colour of the `printed:` and `stderr:` labels, and of nothing else. The same luminance as the name label — identical to two decimal places on dark — and a different hue, so the two labels separate on the blue-yellow axis, which is the one both protanopia and deuteranopia leave intact. Contrast against the editor background is 3.96:1 dark, 3.46:1 light, 11.54:1 high contrast, 7.80:1 high contrast light. Never the error colour: a library warning painted red teaches a student to fear a line that worked.

Contributed, but not currently painted anywhere: #95 gave every annotation state a shared background of its own, `evalens.annotationTint`, so this id has no effect until something is wired back to it. Left in place rather than removed, since a customization already made against it should not silently start failing.
Colour of an inline evaluation error.

Contributed, but not currently painted anywhere: #95 moved the error annotation's background to the same shared `evalens.annotationTint` every other state uses, so this id has no effect until something is wired back to it. Left in place rather than removed, since a customization already made against it should not silently start failing.
Background of the region an evaluation covered.
Colour of the marker beside a statement that has not finished.
Background of the region an evaluation is still running in. Greyed rather than coloured, because there is nothing to read there yet.
Colour of the marker beside a statement blocked on input() -- the reader's turn, not the tool's. Never the error colour: a prompt is not a failure.

Background of the region a statement is blocked on input() in. Loud rather than greyed: nothing moves until the reader answers, and this is meant to be the focal point of the screen for as long as that is true.
Brief emphasis on a region that has just finished. It decays after a moment on purpose: once every line carries a value, what says which one just ran is the change rather than the colour.

Colour of the 3px border on an annotation's leading edge, marking it as a distinct surface from the source line it sits beside — and, on a line where a user's own trailing comment sits right next to near-identical annotation text, the one mark that says where one stops and the other starts. A saturated violet of its own rather than the dim `evalens.labelForeground`, which exists to recede and would make the bar the quietest thing on the row. Only for a value that is currently evaluated: a still-pending annotation is greyed through `evalens.pendingForeground`, a stale one takes its own `evalens.staleBorder` (#109), and an error takes `evalens.errorForeground` unless it is also stale, in which case stale outranks it — so the bar never reads more confidently than the state it marks.

Background wash behind one chip of an annotation — a label and the value it introduces, or `printed:` and its text — so each chip reads as a surface rather than as punctuation. The gap between two chips is left untinted on purpose, so the line still parses into distinct facts. One colour for `evaluated` and `pending` alike, because the accent bar already carries most of the distinction between them — `evalens.staleTint` is the one state with a tint of its own. Computed at 10% opacity of `evalens.resultForeground`'s own hue per theme, so the surface reads as part of the same palette as the text rather than a neutral, unrelated wash, chosen so no foreground colour this extension paints drops below the contrast ratios already asserted for it.

Colour of the 1px hairline that separates two value groups of one continuous annotation (#118) — the rule a plain, untinted gap used to be. Its own id rather than `evalens.annotationBorder`: the leading accent bar answers what state the line is in and switches accordingly, while this divider answers where one fact ends and the next begins, which does not change with state — retuning one through `workbench.colorCustomizations` should not silently retune the other. Computed at 40% opacity of `evalens.resultForeground`'s own hue per theme, the same value colour the tint behind it already uses, so the rule reads as part of the same palette rather than a fifth, unrelated colour.

Background wash behind a stale chip (#109), replacing `evalens.annotationTint` only there. A stale value keeps its own colour — dimming it would put a claim about the value in competition with the value itself — so the surface behind it is the one thing left that can say it has expired. Computed the way `evalens.annotationTint` was, from `evalens.pendingForeground`'s own grey hue rather than the value's, and at roughly half its alpha, so the chip visibly recedes rather than merely changing hue.

Colour of the 3px border on a stale chip's leading edge (#109), replacing `evalens.annotationBorder` only there. The same grey `evalens.pendingForeground` already uses, but its own contributed id rather than that one directly — pending and stale are different claims, not finished yet against finished but out of date, and retuning one through `workbench.colorCustomizations` should not silently retune the other.
